title: The One With The Male Nanny

jokes.text: Monica screaming about her new job: 'You bet your ass I am!'
jokes.setup: Chandler calmly says 'Honey, you're screaming'
jokes.punchline: 'You bet your ass I am!' — Monica fully owns the screaming rather than apologizing
jokes.explanation: Classic Monica energy — her intensity played against Chandler's deadpan. Good character integration, nothing exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Why are you screaming?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You bet your ass I am!

jokes.text: 'And clean? Not just health department-clean, Monica-clean!'
jokes.setup: Monica is raving about her new kitchen
jokes.punchline: She uses herself as the gold standard of cleanliness, obliviously revealing her obsessiveness
jokes.explanation: Sharp and efficient. Only Monica could unselfconsciously coin 'Monica-clean' as a category above health department standards. Strong character integration — the joke IS the character's blind spot about herself.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Jeffrey is so funny! He's got this incredible sense of humor. I haven't laughed this hard at work in years.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh really? That's... that's great. Jeffrey sounds hilarious.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: He really is! He had everyone in the break room cracking up today.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I mean, I can be funny too. I say funny things. People laugh at my jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I know you're funny, Chandler.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Right. Because I'm the funny one. That's kind of my thing.

jokes.text: Monica declares Jeffrey the maitre d' is 'without a doubt the funniest guy I have ever met' — cutting to Chandler's reaction
jokes.setup: Monica is enthusiastically praising her new workplace, then pivots to this superlative claim
jokes.punchline: The audience knows Chandler considers himself 'the funny one' — the camera (or beat) lets this land as a gut punch to his identity
jokes.explanation: Seeds the episode's A-plot conflict economically. The comedy is in what Monica doesn't realize she's said and what Chandler's face must be doing. Effective setup for a longer payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Do you need both hands for holding hands?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, I do.

jokes.text: 'If you were bigger you'd hit me.'
jokes.setup: Mike has been gently teasing Phoebe about whether their relationship is getting serious, making her uncomfortable
jokes.punchline: Mike acknowledges Phoebe's irritation with cheerful self-awareness — implying she'd physically retaliate if she could reach him
jokes.explanation: Economical and charming. Mike's casual read of Phoebe's suppressed violence is delivered with perfect lightness. The 'if you were bigger' implies a height gap and a feistiness about Phoebe that's true to character.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Phoebe, I know we haven't been dating that long, but I really see a future with you.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh... that's... wow.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: I can tell by your expression that you're not quite ready to hear that yet.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No, no, I'm excited! I'm just showing my excited face.

jokes.text: Mike reaches into pocket to give Phoebe something meaningful — produces gum
jokes.setup: Mike builds up to giving Phoebe something important, serious romantic moment
jokes.punchline: 'No, not.. That's gum.'
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom misdirection but executed cleanly. The structure is tight — build genuine romantic tension, deflate with mundane gum. Mike's flustered acknowledgment lands the beat.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: I have something very special to show you.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What is it?

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: It's gum.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: That's... gum?

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Very special gum.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh! Wait, is that money in your pocket?

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: What? No, that's just—

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: How much is it? We could split it!

jokes.text: 'Oh, five bucks! I love it when that happens, you know?'
jokes.setup: Mike tells her to keep digging past the gum
jokes.punchline: Phoebe gets sidetracked finding five dollars and celebrates it, extending the gag before finding the actual key
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the misdirection gag. Phoebe's genuine delight at finding five dollars while Mike is trying to give her an apartment key is characteristically Phoebe — scattered but warm.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm gonna be honest with you, Mike. I'm still a little mad about the gum.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: I know, that's why I'm giving you this key. It's to my apartment.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh. Well, I'm still gonna go with the money.

jokes.text: 'It's a key. To be honest, I think I'd prefer the five dollars.'
jokes.setup: Mike finally reveals it's an apartment key — a major romantic gesture
jokes.punchline: Phoebe jokes she'd rather have the five dollars
jokes.explanation: Callback to the five dollars lands comfortably. Phoebe undercutting a romantic moment with practical humor is in character. Not exceptional but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you guys! Exchanging keys is like, the ultimate symbol of trust and commitment. It means you're letting someone into your life, into your home, into your—

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Wait. Wait, wait, wait. How do they even work? Like, how does this tiny piece of metal know which lock to open?

jokes.text: 'I know it. It is amazing. These little things open doors!'
jokes.setup: Mike and Phoebe have just exchanged keys in a touching moment
jokes.punchline: Phoebe comments with genuine amazement that keys open doors — as if this is a profound revelation
jokes.explanation: Pure Phoebe — she undercuts a sincere romantic scene by being genuinely awed by how keys work. The joke earns its laugh through character specificity; only Phoebe would have this thought at this moment.

dialogue.speaker: Nanny Candidate
dialogue.line: So when you do the random drug testing, how much advance notice do I get?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: ...That's not how random testing works.

dialogue.speaker: Nanny Candidate
dialogue.line: Right, but I'm asking for a courtesy heads-up.

jokes.text: Nanny candidate asks if they do random drug testing, then says she needs three days' notice
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel are wrapping up a nanny interview, thinking it went fine
jokes.punchline: The candidate reveals she'd need three days' notice for drug testing, implying active drug use
jokes.explanation: Classic two-beat setup. The question itself is funny (why would a nanny ask this?), then the second beat twists the knife by specifying she needs advance notice — confirming the implication hilariously. Well-structured, earns a solid laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: The blond with no bra.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I didn't even notice her hair color.

jokes.text: 'What, the blond with no bra?' / 'She was blond?'
jokes.setup: Ross suggests reconsidering their first nanny candidate
jokes.punchline: Rachel noticed no bra; Ross only noticed she was blond — revealing exactly where each of their minds was
jokes.explanation: Sharp exchange. Each character's one-line reveal exposes their different preoccupations economically and credibly. Ross's obliviousness to the more obvious detail is the funnier half.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wow, Sandy has an impressive resume. Let me just meet this person...

dialogue.speaker: Sandy
dialogue.line: [Sandy enters - reveals he is a man]

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh! Sandy's a... you're a guy.

jokes.text: Sandy the nanny is introduced — 'And she's a little mannish'
jokes.setup: Ross reads Sandy's impressive credentials — degree in Early Childhood Education, three years experience — building expectation of a wholesome female nanny
jokes.punchline: Sandy is a man, and Ross's euphemistic 'a little mannish' is the reveal
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom reveal with good structural timing — the credentials buildup earns the visual punchline. 'A little mannish' as understatement for 'he is a man' works in context.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: Oh no, I left my luggage in the cab!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, we can worry about that later. Right now I just want to look at you.

jokes.text: David explains he spent all the grant money and 'accomplished nothing'
jokes.setup: David says he's here to explain to grant funders why the project is going well
jokes.punchline: He immediately corrects course — they spent all the money and accomplished nothing
jokes.explanation: Self-aware self-deprecation with good structural reversal. The pivot from 'why it's a positive thing' to 'accomplished nothing' is the joke. Economical and endearing for the character.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: There's an ancient Russian expression that says... 'You are a person of considerable merit and appeal.'

jokes.text: David left his luggage in the cab
jokes.setup: Phoebe asks 'Where's your luggage?' after David's romantic speech about giving her address to the cab driver
jokes.punchline: David's 'Damn it.' — he was so swept up in romance he forgot his bags
jokes.explanation: Sweet puncturing of romantic idealism. The 'damn it' sells it — David's aware of his own absurdity. Character-specific: only the absent-minded scientist would do this.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I mean, look at me. I'm not exactly...

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You know what? No. I look good. I look really good.

jokes.text: David recites the 'old Russian expression' that roughly translates to 'This thing that I'm looking at: Wow.'
jokes.setup: David says there's an old Russian expression — the audience expects something poetic or profound
jokes.punchline: The translation is literally 'This thing that I'm looking at: Wow' — maximally unpoetic despite the elaborate buildup
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's better jokes. The structure is clean: foreign-language buildup promises something beautiful, the deflation into caveman-simple English is funny and reveals David's charming awkwardness. Character-specific for the bumbling romantic scientist.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, you could have just said yes.

jokes.text: 'You should see me when.. Actually, no, I look pretty good.'
jokes.setup: David says Phoebe looks beautiful; she begins a self-deprecating response then pivots to confident self-compliment
jokes.punchline: She catches herself being modest and immediately overrides it with 'Actually, no, I look pretty good'
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Phoebe — the accidental self-awareness, mid-sentence pivot from modesty to candid vanity. The beat where she almost does the humble thing and then doesn't is lovely and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Irresistible? David is irresistible? Monica chooses Chandler?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, I guess 'irresistible' is one word for it.

jokes.text: Phoebe admits she told David she wasn't seeing anyone when he directly asked
jokes.setup: Phoebe says she couldn't tell David about Mike because he didn't give her a chance. Monica asks 'What do you mean?' Phoebe explains he said 'Are you seeing someone?' and she said 'No.'
jokes.punchline: Monica: 'Well, that would've been your window.'
jokes.explanation: Functional observational comedy — the joke is obvious but Monica's deadpan delivery of the obvious makes it work. Nothing special but gets the point across with mild humor.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh wow, what a coincidence. Here I've been searching my whole life for irony, and there it is.

jokes.text: 'Really? The scientist guy?' / 'Really? Chandler?'
jokes.setup: Phoebe says David is irresistible; Monica is skeptical. Rachel mirrors the skepticism about Chandler.
jokes.punchline: Both women simultaneously undercut each other's men, then awkwardly realize what they've done
jokes.explanation: Very well-constructed parallel exchange. Monica and Rachel both express surprise at each other's men being considered attractive — the structural symmetry is elegant and efficient. Both characters are indicted equally, which is fair and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You have to tell David the truth. It's the right thing to do.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You're right, you're right. I wish I'd asked Joey.

jokes.text: Chandler says 'Continue.' after Monica and Rachel have been implying he's not conventionally attractive
jokes.setup: Monica and Rachel's exchange implies Chandler is an unlikely love interest; he's presumably overheard or walks in
jokes.punchline: 'Continue.' — Chandler stoically inviting more insults with a one-word deadpan
jokes.explanation: One word, perfectly deployed. Chandler's masochistic self-awareness — inviting continued mockery — is core to his character. Maximum economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm funny. I'm a funny guy. I make people laugh all the time.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, shut up, door. What do you know about comedy anyway? You just stand there looking stupid.

jokes.text: Phoebe responds to 'isn't it ironic' with 'given my lifelong search for irony, you can imagine how happy I am'
jokes.setup: Monica tries to point out the irony of David arriving the same day Mike gave Phoebe his key
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's biting sarcasm — 'given my lifelong search for irony' — is funnier because Phoebe is rarely this sharp
jokes.explanation: Decent sarcasm from Phoebe, slightly against type which gives it a little edge. But the joke itself is a fairly conventional 'isn't it ironic / oh wow great' structure.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know what I just realized? Oklahoma has a panhandle. But what about the other states? Like, why doesn't Texas have a body part? I mean, it's big enough. It could have... an arm. Or a leg.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: And Florida — Florida's already got the Keys. Why not give it some fingers? 'Hey, let's go to Florida, hang out on the fingers!'

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: But then you get to the really weird ones. Like, what if Nebraska had... a butt? 'Welcome to Nebraska, home of the cornfield and our state butt!'

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: And I'm not even going to tell you what I think Wyoming should have.

jokes.text: 'I knew I should've had this conversation with Joey.'
jokes.setup: Monica insists Phoebe must tell David about Mike; Phoebe explores the 'complicated moral situation / no right, no wrong' loophole
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's conclusion that Joey would've been more sympathetic to her moral dodging
jokes.explanation: Good laugh through implication — the audience knows Joey would absolutely enable Phoebe's bad decision. Efficient joke that uses an absent character for the punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know what I hate? Words that are combinations of other words, like 'y'all'. It's lazy!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: And now everyone's doing it. 'Gonna', 'wanna', 'fricken'...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Fricken! That's not even a real word!

jokes.text: Chandler talking to a door: 'What do you know? You're a door. You just like knock-knock jokes.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is pacing, insecure about being funny, talking to himself — he says 'I'm funny, right?' and then addresses the door
jokes.punchline: 'You're a door. You just like knock-knock jokes.' — an absurdly logical joke about a door preferring knock-knock jokes
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. Chandler's comedic insecurity leads him to seek validation from a door, then immediately deploys a solid wordplay observation about doors/knock-knock jokes. It's funny on two levels: the absurdity of talking to a door AND the actual quality of the door joke. Very Chandler — he can't stop making jokes even when spiraling.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: He does this whole bit about Liza Minnelli, where he's like, pretending to be her, and he's doing all these crazy impressions and movements, and then suddenly he just stops and stares at you with this completely insane look on his face.

jokes.text: Chandler's Oklahoma stand-up bit: 'They call it the Sooner State. Frankly, I'd sooner be in any other state!'
jokes.setup: Chandler is warming up with an Oklahoma joke to impress Monica before meeting Jeffrey
jokes.punchline: 'Frankly, I'd sooner be in any other state' — a groan-worthy pun on 'Sooner'
jokes.explanation: Intentionally weak joke — Chandler is trying too hard and the material is hacky. The meta-joke IS that his prepared material is bad, which is moderately funny, but the actual pun is a groaner with no real craft.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Were you there when Jeffrey did his bit about the fricken thing?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, I was there. That was great. Really original. I wish I had thought of that.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Hey, yeah, I'm from the waistband of Wyoming. But when I was 7, we headed over to the crotch.'
jokes.setup: Chandler builds on the panhandle joke — 'can all states have stuff like that?'
jokes.punchline: Waistband → crotch geography escalation
jokes.explanation: Mild escalation that gets a chuckle. The body-part geography conceit is mildly clever but not developed enough to be memorable. Functions as filler to illustrate Chandler's desperation.

dialogue.speaker: Sandy
dialogue.line: I'm really struggling with leaving my baby with a nanny. I feel so guilty.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Is the nanny hot?

jokes.text: Chandler's Wyoming 'waistband' and 'crotch' geography bit
jokes.setup: Chandler riffs on states having geographic features named like body parts — 'panhandle'
jokes.punchline: 'Hey, I'm from the waistband of Wyoming. But when I was 7, we headed over to the crotch.'
jokes.explanation: Better than the Sooner State joke — the escalation from 'waistband' to 'crotch' has a pleasing logic and mild shock value. Still intentionally hacky material, but funnier than the previous beat.

jokes.text: 'Your new poodle could be your noodle. And fried chicken could be fricken. Waiter? I'll have the fricken!'
jokes.setup: Chandler is riffing on combining words like 'y'all'
jokes.punchline: 'Fricken' as a portmanteau of 'fried chicken' — Chandler acting out ordering it at a restaurant
jokes.explanation: More of Chandler's warm-up material that's intentionally mediocre to contrast with Jeffrey. 'Fricken' gets a mild laugh but the joke exists more as setup for Monica's deflating response.

dialogue.speaker: Sandy
dialogue.line: I just want to make a meaningful connection with a child, you know? To really matter in someone's life.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, you could always just have kids of your own.

jokes.text: Jeffrey's bit: 'Liza Minnelli locked in our freezer eating a raw chicken'
jokes.setup: Monica describes Jeffrey's comedy bit to Chandler
jokes.punchline: The bit itself is surrealist nonsense — 'Liza Minnelli locked in our freezer eating a raw chicken' — with no real logic
jokes.explanation: The joke works on a meta level — the described 'bit' is so random it's funny precisely because it makes no sense, which also makes us unsure if Jeffrey is actually funnier than Chandler. The specific details (Liza Minnelli, freezer, raw chicken) are absurdist image comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, uh, okay. The male equivalent of a Queen would be a King.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: A King?!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yes!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross, a Queen is a woman who rules a kingdom. A King is a man who rules a kingdom.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh. Oh! ...Right, well, that didn't come out right.

jokes.text: 'No, but it sounds fricken funny.'
jokes.setup: Monica describes Jeffrey's Liza Minnelli bit and says 'you probably had to be there'
jokes.punchline: Chandler uses 'fricken' — his own earlier coinage — as a callback insult/endorsement, reclaiming his own joke
jokes.explanation: Smart callback — Chandler uses his own coined word sarcastically to describe Jeffrey's material, managing to be funny while being petty. The circular structure rewards attentive viewers. Good economy and self-aware character work.

dialogue.speaker: Sandy
dialogue.line: I've been doing Monica's nails, helping Rachel with her skincare routine, and I even French-braided Phoebe's hair!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wait, you know how to do all that?

dialogue.speaker: Sandy
dialogue.line: Of course! I'm great with kids.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Right, but... you know about makeup and hair and nails and... all of that?

dialogue.speaker: Sandy
dialogue.line: Yeah, why? What's the problem?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No problem! I just... I didn't know you were into that kind of thing.

dialogue.speaker: Sandy
dialogue.line: Well, I'm a nanny. Part of taking care of kids is knowing this stuff.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Sure, sure. It's just... I don't know. It's weird.

jokes.text: Ross asks Sandy 'Are you gay?' mid-nanny interview
jokes.setup: Sandy has just said something tender about how 'it's like leaving behind a piece of your heart' regarding Rachel's bond with Emma — a genuinely sweet moment
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately blurts 'Are you gay?' — breaking the warm atmosphere with blunt suspicion
jokes.explanation: Cringe comedy with good timing. Ross's inability to process a sensitive male disrupts a sweet moment in the most socially awkward way. The abruptness of the question after Sandy's speech is what makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wait, so you... you know about fabric softener? And you actually care about thread count?

dialogue.speaker: Sandy
dialogue.line: Yeah, of course. Egyptian cotton is really the way to go.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: But you're a guy. A straight guy. How is this possible? Did you hit your head? Are you feeling okay?

jokes.text: 'I'm sorry, that's our Ross. He's just Mr. Shoot Straight From The Hip.'
jokes.setup: Ross has just asked the nanny candidate 'Are you gay?' out of nowhere
jokes.punchline: Rachel's desperate damage control, using an absurdly cheerful euphemism for Ross's social catastrophe
jokes.explanation: Standard cringe-comedy save attempt. Rachel's euphemism for Ross's behavior is functional but not particularly inventive.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could you BE any more of an actor?

jokes.text: 'So you're just, like, a guy who's a nanny.'
jokes.setup: Sandy has explained he's straight, engaged, etc.
jokes.punchline: Ross still can't get past the core concept, reducing it to 'just, like, a guy who's a nanny' — not an insult, just pure unprocessed confusion
jokes.explanation: Ross processing the concept like it's novel physics. The 'just, like' filler captures his bafflement authentically.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, if Chandler didn't have humor, he'd have nothing.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hey!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm just saying, what else you got?

jokes.text: Sandy tears up telling the story of little Daniel and his name 'Skadandy' — Ross and Rachel awkwardly react
jokes.setup: Sandy tells a touching story about a child he nannied — it's genuinely sweet
jokes.punchline: Sandy starts crying; Ross and Rachel visibly don't know how to handle a grown man crying in their living room
jokes.explanation: First deployment of the Sandy-crying gag. Establishes the running pattern. Mildly funny but sets up better payoffs later.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh! A fireman came into the coffee shop the other day. Oh, oh! And he ordered a coffee. And it was huge! It was this big!

jokes.text: 'It's okay. Yeah, kids say all kinds of crap.'
jokes.setup: Sandy is emotionally recounting the child calling him 'Skadandy' as a touching moment
jokes.punchline: Ross deflects with the most dismissive possible response: 'kids say all kinds of crap'
jokes.explanation: Perfect tonal clash — Sandy is emotional and Ross just wants to move past it, so he reaches for the most practical, least sympathetic thing possible. 'All kinds of crap' is exactly the wrong response in context, which makes it right as comedy.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: You're happy with Mike? That's... that's great.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: No wait, it's not great. It's terrible.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: Actually, you know what? It IS great. You deserve to be happy.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: But not with him! With me!

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: I'm being selfish. I'm happy for you. Really.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: No I'm not, I'm miserable.

jokes.text: 'They're mine.' (about the dinosaur toys) — then Sandy's reaction that they're 'also not age-appropriate'
jokes.setup: Sandy picks up dinosaur toys and says they aren't age-appropriate for Emma
jokes.punchline: Ross reveals they're his; Sandy judges that too
jokes.explanation: Very economical two-beat joke. Ross owning the dinosaurs is true to character (paleontologist) and funny on its own; Sandy's calm second judgment 'also not age-appropriate' doubles the joke without over-explaining. Great structure.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Telling you was hard.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: Well, you know, in Swedish culture, we have a concept called 'Janteloven' - it means you're not supposed to think you're better than anyone else. But I think what you're experiencing is the opposite - a kind of emotional vulnerability that transcends cultural boundaries.

jokes.text: Ross argues against a male nanny: 'What kind of a job is that for a man? A nanny? I mean, it's like if a woman wanted to be...' [pause] '...King?'
jokes.setup: Ross is building to a comparison to illustrate how inappropriate male nannying is
jokes.punchline: He can't think of a comparable female-inappropriate job and blurts out 'King?' — immediately exposing the flaws in his own argument
jokes.explanation: Smart comedy — Ross's argument defeats itself in real time. The pause before 'King?' shows his brain working and failing, and the word 'King' is both unexpected and perfectly logical within his failed analogy. Good character work: Ross is revealed as holding a bias he can't even coherently defend.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: In some countries, they greet each other with a kiss on the lips.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh! Which ones?

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: Uh, all of them.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, okay!

jokes.text: Sandy uses Monica's homemade calendula and honey lotion on Emma — 'Plus, it keeps the hands young.'
jokes.setup: Sandy has taken care of Emma's diaper AND brought homemade lotion for her rash
jokes.punchline: He adds the detail that the lotion also keeps hands young — a vanity detail from a male nanny that surprises
jokes.explanation: Light character-building joke for Sandy. The pivot from functional (rash treatment) to cosmetic (young hands) is a small surprise. Functions to build Sandy's overly perfect persona.

dialogue.speaker: Sandy
dialogue.line: So I got down on one knee, and I said, 'Will you marry me?'

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh my God, that's so romantic!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, what happened next?

dialogue.speaker: Sandy
dialogue.line: Well, she started crying...

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh, hey, you know what? I just remembered I have to... feed my fish.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah, and I have to... wash my hair. All of it.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Right now?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It's urgent.

jokes.text: Rachel hires Sandy immediately: 'Yes! Sandy, you're hired!' — then Sandy cries again at being welcomed
jokes.setup: Sandy has just demonstrated his qualifications perfectly
jokes.punchline: Sandy immediately tears up again at being welcomed into a family — running gag escalation
jokes.explanation: Second Sandy-crying beat. Less surprising than the first but confirms the running gag. The 'come here' hug from Rachel adds to the comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Sandy has cried more than I have.

jokes.text: 'You gotta be at least bi.'
jokes.setup: Sandy has just cried and hugged Rachel; Ross has watched this whole sequence
jokes.punchline: Ross's quiet aside, still unable to accept a straight male nanny
jokes.explanation: Good callback to Ross's earlier question. He's escalated his certainty slightly — from 'are you gay?' to 'at least bi.' The quiet aside delivery makes it funnier than the blurted question.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Sandy's making madeleines. Madeleines! Those are girl cookies.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: A guy should eat cookies with chunks in them. Chocolate chips, nuts, maybe some pretzel pieces.

jokes.text: Chandler asks Joey to set him up for a joke about fire trucks when Monica's around — Joey says he's 'not so good with remembering lines'
jokes.setup: Chandler needs a straight man for a prepared joke to impress Monica
jokes.punchline: Joey — a professional actor — admits he's 'not so good with remembering lines'
jokes.explanation: Excellent character-specific irony. Joey is a professional actor who cannot remember lines — this is an established character trait elevated here by perfect context. Chandler asking an actor to remember one line and the actor's admission of incompetence is a sharp joke with deep character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Sandy's too sensitive. She cries at everything.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross, you're not exactly a rugged cowboy yourself. You cried during a commercial last week.

jokes.text: 'Thank God your livelihood doesn't depend on it.'
jokes.setup: Joey admits he's 'not so good with remembering lines'
jokes.punchline: Chandler's withering response — sarcastically grateful that Joey's career doesn't depend on the very thing he just said he can't do
jokes.explanation: Chandler's sarcasm at its sharpest. The irony is multi-layered — it's funny because Joey's livelihood absolutely DOES depend on remembering lines, and Joey doesn't catch it. 'Thank God' is pitch-perfect deadpan. One of the episode's best lines.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: We can't keep kissing.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: Why not? I have a theory. The key to understanding human behavior is recognizing that we are all, fundamentally, slaves to our biological impulses. Therefore, kissing is not a choice—it's a necessity. A physiological imperative.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: That's not a theory, that's an excuse.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: Is it? Or is it both?

jokes.text: 'I know, right?' — Joey agreeing with Chandler's sarcastic statement
jokes.setup: Chandler says sarcastically 'Thank God your livelihood doesn't depend on it'
jokes.punchline: Joey agrees sincerely — completely missing the sarcasm
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the previous joke. Joey's sincere 'I know, right?' lands because it confirms he's completely unaware of the irony. Character-perfect for Joey and maximally efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So what does Sandy do all day with Ben?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh, uh, well, this morning they made sachets.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Sachets?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, little scented pouches. And then, uh, this afternoon they're gonna do some light vacuuming and maybe see some Christmas lights.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Christmas lights? It's not even Thanksgiving yet!

jokes.text: 'No! Being funny's your thing! Without that, you just got lame with women!'
jokes.setup: Joey is validating Chandler's concern about losing his identity as 'the funny one'
jokes.punchline: Joey's 'support' inadvertently reveals that Chandler's only redeeming quality (beyond funny) is apparently nothing good — 'lame with women'
jokes.explanation: Joey trying to be supportive and accidentally insulting Chandler further is a reliable comedy engine for these two. The specificity of 'lame with women' (not just 'lame') is the right amount of precise insult.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It's like when you have a really nice apartment...

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Don't do it, Joey.

jokes.text: Joey blurts 'Fire trucks!' the moment Monica enters — before Chandler has set up the joke
jokes.setup: Chandler has asked Joey to say 'fire trucks' when Monica comes in, as a setup line for Chandler's joke
jokes.punchline: Joey immediately says 'Fire trucks!' the moment he sees Monica, before any context is established
jokes.explanation: Joey's inability to follow even the simplest instruction ('say it when I'm telling a joke') is perfectly in character — he remembers the word but not the context. The random 'Fire trucks!' with no setup is funnier than any fire truck joke Chandler could have told.

jokes.text: David brings Phoebe lemon vodka from Minsk — 'I traded four pairs of Levi's for that.' / 'Yeah, we actually have this here.'
jokes.setup: David proudly presents an exotic gift — lemon-flavored vodka from Minsk
jokes.punchline: Phoebe gently reveals it's readily available in New York; David reveals the significant cost (four pairs of Levi's) of this commonplace item
jokes.explanation: Sweet and funny. The 'four pairs of Levi's' detail is specific enough to be absurd — David values Phoebe enough to trade significant goods for something freely available in her city. Reveals both his effort and the gap between Minsk and New York.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: He's smart, he's funny, he's a paleontologist...

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: But a father?

jokes.text: David announces 'I'm going to kiss you now' — Phoebe says 'Wait' — David: 'I can't get away with stuff like that. It sounded sexy in my head.'
jokes.setup: David builds romantic tension, then announces his intention to kiss Phoebe
jokes.punchline: He immediately loses his nerve and self-diagnoses: 'I can't get away with stuff like that. It sounded sexy in my head.'
jokes.explanation: Perfectly captures David's character — bookish, sincere, slightly deluded about his own cool. 'It sounded sexy in my head' is an eminently quotable line that captures romantic self-awareness in a funny, specific way. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: A male nanny? What do you call that?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: A manny!

jokes.text: David's rapid emotional volley: 'Damn it. I'm sorry. I want you to be happy. But only with me. No, that's not fair. Who cares. Leave him. I don't mean that. Yes, I do. I'm sorry.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe tells David she is happy with Mike
jokes.punchline: David cycles through every emotional response in rapid succession, contradicting himself with each beat
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best David moments. The compressed emotional spiral is both funny and genuinely human. Each contradiction comes faster than the last, building real comedic momentum. 'Who cares. Leave him.' snuck into the middle is the peak. Character-specific for a man whose intellectual self-awareness can't quite control his heart.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: A man nanny? What's next, a man nurse? A man... manicurist?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I mean, I'm okay with it, but I'm not changing any diapers.

jokes.text: 'Well, just so you know, hearing it wasn't exactly a Vladnik carnival, either.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe says telling David about Mike was 'one of the hardest things I've ever had to do'
jokes.punchline: David's dry response uses an invented Minsk cultural reference — 'Vladnik carnival' — as his unit of fun
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best-crafted lines. 'Vladnik carnival' is a wholly invented cultural reference that works perfectly — it sounds plausible, it's funny purely as a phrase, and David using it as his baseline for fun says everything about his world. The dry understatement of the delivery matches the structure of the line perfectly. This is what good guest-character writing looks like: funny, specific, and character-revealing.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. You were faking it? You were faking laughing at my jokes?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God. OH MY GOD! You were faking it!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: How long? How long have you been faking it?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Since we've been together?! SINCE WE'VE BEEN TOGETHER?!

jokes.text: David attempts the Minsk goodbye custom: 'In Minsk? It's two on each cheek and one on the lips.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe agrees a cheek kiss wouldn't be 'totally inappropriate' as a goodbye
jokes.punchline: David invents/invokes a Minsk custom to justify a lips kiss — Phoebe almost goes along with it
jokes.explanation: Classic romantic-comedy maneuver played with awareness. David's escalating kiss count under the guise of Minsk customs is transparent and charming. 'Well, if that's what they do in Minsk' from Phoebe — almost falling for it — is the right straight-man response.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: There once was a man from Peru, who dreamed of a girl he once knew. She had raven black hair, and a delicate flair, but he cried when he thought of her, boo hoo.

jokes.text: 'Do you realize that man has cried in our apartment three times? I haven't cried that many times since I moved in!'
jokes.setup: Ross is complaining about Sandy crying
jokes.punchline: Ross's comparison — using his own crying frequency as a low bar — inadvertently admits he cries in his own apartment
jokes.explanation: Smart double reveal — Ross is criticizing Sandy for crying while accidentally admitting he cries regularly too. The self-incrimination is unintentional and therefore funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's so funny, Joey!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Thanks, but I can't take credit for that. Chandler said it.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah. I just repeated it because I thought it was funny. I do that sometimes—I hear something good and I repeat it like I came up with it.

jokes.text: 'Come on, Ross, you got a little misty when Ben broke your I-heart-fossils mug.'
jokes.setup: Ross says he hasn't cried that much since moving in
jokes.punchline: Rachel has specific receipts — the 'I Heart Fossils' mug broken by Ben
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'I Heart Fossils' as a mug is perfect character work. Only Ross would have this mug, only Ross would cry over it, and Rachel recalling the specific incident is both good comedy and good character interaction.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, that's not my lipstick. We're just in a synchronized lipstick phase right now. It's like when couples start to look alike, except with cosmetics. It means we're connected on a deeper level.

jokes.text: 'I'll have you know that was a farewell gift from my colleagues at the museum. They all chipped in for that.' / 'They must have all loved you very much.'
jokes.setup: Ross defends his emotional attachment to the mug
jokes.punchline: Rachel's 'They must have all loved you very much' — delivered with sympathy that subtly implies collective mediocrity of the gift
jokes.explanation: Rachel's faux-sympathetic response works as gentle condescension. The implication is that if many colleagues chipped in for a simple mug, it wasn't a great showing of affection. Mild but functional.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm done with this!

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Oh, so now you're just leaving?

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: Yes, and you know why? Because you pointed at me!

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: I pointed at you?

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: WITH YOUR FINGER!

jokes.text: 'What kind of a guy makes delicate French cookies? They're not even butch, manly cookies with.. You know, with chunks!'
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to articulate why Sandy bothers him
jokes.punchline: He invents the category of 'butch, manly cookies with chunks' as the alternative Sandy should be making
jokes.explanation: 'Butch, manly cookies with chunks' is the kind of absurdist specificity that elevates a complaint into genuine comedy. Ross has constructed an entire masculine baking aesthetic in his head. The vagueness of 'chunks' — what kind of chunks? — adds to the absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: Well, if you do go to Minsk, I'd recommend visiting the National Library. It's quite beautiful. And the Stalin Museum is fascinating from a historical perspective.

jokes.text: 'I gotta tell you, Ross, it's not like you just came in from branding cattle.'
jokes.setup: Ross is defending his right to critique Sandy's masculinity
jokes.punchline: Rachel points out that Ross himself is not exactly a rugged masculine standard
jokes.explanation: 'Branding cattle' is a nice specific image — it's not 'you're not very manly,' it's a vivid picture of what Ross is definitely not. Good character-based insult.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Joey, that's not 'Hot Cross Buns.' That's 'Mary Had a Little Lamb.'

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No way, man. I'm totally nailing this. Listen.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: This is definitely 'Hot Cross Buns.'

jokes.text: Ross defends his manliness: 'I play squash!'
jokes.setup: Ross says 'as a kid, I wasn't the athlete I am now'
jokes.punchline: 'I play squash!' — Ross's evidence of athletic masculinity is squash, an upper-crust racquet sport
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-word punchline. Squash as Ross's athletic credential is exactly right — elite enough to feel unearned as a masculinity claim, specific enough to be true to character. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Sandy
dialogue.line: I'd like you to meet Mr. Wigglemunch and the Grumpus.

jokes.text: Ross and Sandy's scene: Ross is unable to explain what 'too sensitive' is — the scene fades to Sandy comforting a crying Ross
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to articulate why Sandy is 'too sensitive' as a reason to fire him
jokes.punchline: Sandy turns the tables by asking Ross probing questions about his father and his childhood, until Ross is the one crying
jokes.explanation: The episode's comedic centerpiece. The structure is elegant: Ross spends the whole episode judging Sandy for being too sensitive, then Sandy (the nanny) turns the tables and emotionally excavates Ross until Ross is the one crying. It's a perfect ironic reversal that earns everything it's been building toward. The escalation from 'my father,' to dinosaurs, to tank tops is well-paced. Character-perfect for Ross, who famously has daddy issues and deep emotional vulnerabilities beneath a blustery exterior. This is the episode's best joke sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Sandy
dialogue.line: Who wants to play with puppets?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh, me! Me! I love puppets!

jokes.text: Mike: 'And you, thanks for the face massage!' to David, noting Phoebe's lipstick is on David's mouth
jokes.setup: Mike has pieced together what happened — Phoebe's lipstick is on David's mouth
jokes.punchline: He sarcastically thanks David for the 'face massage' — a pointed, dry accusation that acknowledges the situation without saying it directly
jokes.explanation: Mike's 'face massage' is a sharp, economical way to call out the kiss without confronting it directly. The sarcasm is specific enough to be funny and the euphemism does real comic work.

dialogue.speaker: Sandy
dialogue.line: Ross, you'll be the grumpy puppet!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Why do I have to be the grumpy one?

dialogue.speaker: Sandy
dialogue.line: Because you're perfect for it!

jokes.text: Joey completes the 'it's like a woman wanting to be...' sentence with 'A penis model!'
jokes.setup: Ross started a sentence about gender-inappropriate jobs ('it's like a woman wanting to be...') and couldn't finish it; now Joey completes it
jokes.punchline: 'A penis model!' — the most Joey answer imaginable
jokes.explanation: Callback payoff to Ross's failed analogy. Joey's answer reveals that (a) he's thought about this profession specifically, (b) he considers it legitimate, (c) it's gender-appropriate in his mind. Perfect character specificity — only Joey would say this. The long pause before the callback makes the punchline land harder.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: She's not a real person! She's a fictional character created by P.L. Travers!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ross, what's wrong with Mary Poppins?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What's wrong with her? She's practically perfect in every way! That's psychologically unrealistic. Nobody's that perfect. It's Gary Poppins!

jokes.text: 'Really? Do you not know Chandler?'
jokes.setup: Monica is surprised Chandler would be jealous of a co-worker being called funny
jokes.punchline: Joey's rhetorical question implies that anyone who knows Chandler should understand this insecurity perfectly
jokes.explanation: Economical and delivered with Joey's particular blend of loyalty and casual roasting. 'Do you not know Chandler?' implies years of witnessing this exact insecurity.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: My new email address is ChandellerBing@tulsa-sucks-and-jeffreys-a-jerk.com

jokes.text: Joey lists Ross's qualities: 'Science? Academia? Being a good father?' — all with trailing uncertainty
jokes.setup: Monica says 'Being funny is Chandler's thing. Like Ross's thing is...' and trails off. Joey fills in.
jokes.punchline: Joey can only come up with vague academic labels, each delivered as a tentative question rather than a confident answer
jokes.explanation: The uncertainty in Joey's suggestions (all as questions) implies Ross's identity is genuinely unclear even to his best friends. Mild but lands with awareness of the characters.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Sandy, I'm going to have to let you go.

dialogue.speaker: Sandy
dialogue.line: But why? What did I do wrong?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It's not you, it's just... you're like SpongeBob SquarePants.

dialogue.speaker: Sandy
dialogue.line: I don't understand.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Everyone loves SpongeBob, but nobody wants to actually work with him.

jokes.text: 'That's like Chandler saying he met someone who was more uptight than you.' / 'Excuse me?' / 'I'm sorry. Sorry. More controlling than you.' / 'Well, that's better.'
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to explain Chandler's feelings using an analogy involving Monica
jokes.punchline: He calls Monica 'uptight,' corrects to 'controlling' on her objection — and Monica accepts 'controlling' as a better description of herself
jokes.explanation: Very well-constructed exchange. The joke builds in two beats: (1) Monica objects to 'uptight,' and (2) she accepts 'controlling' as fair — which is funnier because she's tacitly accepting that the insult itself is correct, just the wrong word. Good character revelation.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: This is your fault! Why did you have to be so charming?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Me? I didn't do anything!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Exactly! You just stood there being all... you, and now Sandy likes us better than everyone else!

jokes.text: 'You got a man who's a nanny? You got a manny?'
jokes.setup: Ross explains they hired a male nanny
jokes.punchline: Joey coins 'manny' — portmanteau of man + nanny
jokes.explanation: The portmanteau works and is delivered with Joey's authentic delight at coining something. 'Manny' is both funny and genuinely usable — it became a real word in public discourse partly due to this episode. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I wasn't athletic as a kid.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Really? What changed?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, I can still do it if I want to.

jokes.text: 'You know, I don't mind a male nanny, but I do draw the line at male wet nurse.'
jokes.setup: Joey has accepted the concept of a manny
jokes.punchline: He draws a principled line at 'male wet nurse' — a comparably absurd but physically impossible concept he has apparently considered
jokes.explanation: Joey's particular code of ethics is always funny — his flexible acceptance of 'manny' but firm rejection of 'male wet nurse' implies he has a nuanced internal framework for gender roles that extends to breastfeeding. Character-specific absurdism.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I was just exploring the geomorphology of the dinosaurs' natural habitat!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It was a very educational experience.

jokes.text: Monica laughs extravagantly at Joey's joke — 'You are on a roll, mister!'
jokes.setup: Joey has made a joke; Monica laughs enthusiastically
jokes.punchline: This immediately sets up the cruelty — Monica laughs at Joey but Chandler's earlier jokes got nothing
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the contrast — Monica effortlessly laughs at Joey's joke, oblivious to what this does to Chandler. Functional setup for Chandler's realization.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Why can't men wear tank tops? Why is that not socially acceptable? I have very nice arms!

jokes.text: Chandler realizes Monica's laughs were pity laughs — 'Pity laughs?!'
jokes.setup: Monica has been caught having pity-laughed at Chandler's jokes
jokes.punchline: Chandler's horror at the concept — the exact thing he feared (not being genuinely funny) has been confirmed
jokes.explanation: Good cringe beat — Chandler's worst fear realized. The repetition of 'pity laughs' captures his processing the concept in real time.

jokes.text: 'I do limericks. There once was a man named Chandler whose wife made him die inside.'
jokes.setup: Monica says Jeffrey does bits, impressions, and limericks; Chandler insists he does limericks too
jokes.punchline: His limerick example begins with 'There once was a man named Chandler whose wife made him die inside' — immediately going to dark marital complaint
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and most quotable lines. Chandler proving he can do limericks by producing one that reveals his current emotional state — 'his wife made him die inside' — is perfectly constructed. It's funny on two levels: the limerick form makes dark feelings absurdly formal, and the content itself reveals Chandler's comedic way of processing pain. This is what 8+ looks like: character-specific, formally clever, and emotionally true.

jokes.text: Monica tells the Jerry Lewis/girl with lazy eye joke — she thinks she made it up
jokes.setup: Monica tries to prove Chandler is funny by citing a joke that 'slayed' her last week
jokes.punchline: Chandler: 'Hey! I made up that joke and told it to you.' Monica has forgotten the source of a joke she loved
jokes.explanation: Monica's well-intentioned support paradoxically demonstrates her obliviousness — the joke she loved was his, and she forgot. Good beat that earns Chandler's frustration.

dialogue.speaker: Sandy
dialogue.line: Why did the cookie go to the doctor? Because it felt crumbly!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That's... that's amazing! How do you come up with this stuff?

dialogue.speaker: Sandy
dialogue.line: It's just a silly joke, Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Silly? SILLY?! Sandy, you should be charging for this. Do you know how much Yale costs? You could be doing this full-time. You're basically running an educational institution here.

jokes.text: 'Not knowing when to shut up. Yep, that's my thing.'
jokes.setup: Monica realizes she's been digging herself deeper
jokes.punchline: Chandler concedes that his real 'thing' is 'not knowing when to shut up'
jokes.explanation: Chandler's self-deprecating acceptance is a good button. 'That's my thing' said with resignation is very Chandler — using humor to absorb a painful truth.

jokes.text: 'So how many guys have your key?' — Mike arrives to find Phoebe with David's lipstick on her
jokes.setup: Mike lets himself in with his new key to find Phoebe in a compromising state from kissing David
jokes.punchline: 'So how many guys have your key?' — a dry question that undercuts the romantic gesture of exchanging keys from earlier
jokes.explanation: Smart callback — Mike uses the newly exchanged key to arrive at the worst possible moment, then makes a dry joke about it. The irony of the key being used to discover a betrayal is a nice structural payoff to the episode's opening scene.

jokes.text: 'Your lipstick's on his mouth.' / 'We just happen to wear the same shade.'
jokes.setup: Mike points out Phoebe's lipstick is on David's mouth
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's desperate cover story: they wear the same lipstick shade
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's terrible lie is delivered with her signature earnest desperation. The audience knows it's absurd; Phoebe seems to briefly believe it might work.

jokes.text: Mike and David's confrontation: 'What are you gonna do about it?' / 'Well, I'll show you what I'm gonna do about it' — two clearly non-threatening men squaring up
jokes.setup: David and Mike are about to fight over Phoebe
jokes.punchline: Two bookish, non-physical men performing the choreography of a fight they clearly cannot have
jokes.explanation: Classic romantic comedy trope — the awkward men's fight. Functional but not especially inventive.

jokes.text: David's exit threat: 'If I ever do come back from Minsk, well, you just better watch out.'
jokes.setup: David is making a dramatic exit after the fight
jokes.punchline: His threat is immediately undercut by the conditional 'if I ever do come back from Minsk' — an indefinite and uncertain threat
jokes.explanation: David undermines his own threat by embedding geographic uncertainty into it. Character-perfect — he's too honest and self-aware to commit to a threat he may not be able to follow through on.

jokes.text: David gives Mike his phone number: 'If you do ever come to Minsk, that's my number. We'll party up Vladnik-style.'
jokes.setup: David says goodbye to Phoebe and Mike after the confrontation
jokes.punchline: He gives his number to the man he was just fighting over Phoebe with, inviting him to 'party Vladnik-style'
jokes.explanation: Excellent closing beat for David's arc. He transitions from romantic rival to potential friend in a single gesture, and 'Vladnik-style' callbacks perfectly to 'Vladnik carnival' from earlier. David's bizarre social grace — turning a fight into a party invitation — is both funny and oddly lovable. One of the episode's best moments for the guest character.

jokes.text: Joey has learned 'Hot Cross Buns' on recorder — Ross says it sounded like 'Three Blind Mice' — Sandy demonstrates Three Blind Mice
jokes.setup: Joey triumphantly announces Sandy taught him 'Hot Cross Buns' on recorder
jokes.punchline: Ross says it sounded like 'Three Blind Mice'; Sandy immediately plays Three Blind Mice to demonstrate the difference — implying Ross was right
jokes.explanation: Light gag about Joey's musical incompetence. The visual of Sandy playing recorder to demonstrate Three Blind Mice is mildly funny; Ross's weary 'I swear to God' sells it.

jokes.text: Ross asks 'How exactly is a 2-month-old supposed to appreciate puppets?' — Sandy explains cerebral development — 'The whimsical characters are just for us.'
jokes.setup: Ross is skeptical that puppets benefit a 2-month-old
jokes.punchline: Sandy validates Ross's concern but admits the puppet characters themselves are for the adults — specifically not denying that he (a grown man) made them for his own enjoyment
jokes.explanation: 'The whimsical characters are just for us' — Sandy's honest admission that he made puppets for adult-Sandy's enjoyment, delivered with complete sincerity, is in character and mildly funny.

jokes.text: Joey yells 'I want to be Mr. Wigglemunch!'
jokes.setup: Sandy asks who wants to be Mr. Wigglemunch and who wants to be the Grumpus
jokes.punchline: Joey immediately and eagerly claims Mr. Wigglemunch — again, more engaged than the baby
jokes.explanation: Joey claiming Mr. Wigglemunch with adult competitive enthusiasm implies Ross gets stuck being the Grumpus, which is perfect casting. Light but satisfying.

jokes.text: 'Well, I guess we know who's gonna be the Grumpus!'
jokes.setup: Joey has claimed Mr. Wigglemunch; Ross is standing by disapprovingly
jokes.punchline: Sandy's cheerful observation that Ross — who has been grumpy all episode — is naturally the Grumpus
jokes.explanation: Good payoff — Sandy has perfectly identified Ross as the Grumpus without malice, which makes it funnier. The thematic resonance with Ross being the episode's grump is clean.

jokes.text: Sandy: 'Oh, my God. Well, I guess we know who's gonna be the Grumpus!'
jokes.setup: Joey has eagerly claimed Wigglemunch, leaving only the Grumpus for someone
jokes.punchline: Sandy calls out the obvious — the person still scowling and resistant is the Grumpus
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the puppet setup — Ross is obviously the Grumpus. Sandy saying it out loud is the punchline. It works because Sandy says it cheerfully, as a neutral observation, which makes it land as more of a dig than if someone else said it.

jokes.text: 'I'm sorry I'm the only one who isn't in love with Gary Poppins out there.'
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to explain his discomfort with Sandy to Rachel
jokes.punchline: 'Gary Poppins' — Ross's nickname for Sandy, blending 'Mary Poppins' with a masculine name
jokes.explanation: 'Gary Poppins' is an excellent coinage — specific, memorable, and doing real work. It captures both Sandy's nannying excellence and Ross's gendered discomfort with a single invented name. High quotability.

jokes.text: Chandler's exit line: 'So if your maitre d' friend has any funny Oklahoma jokes, tell him to e-mail me at www-dot-ha-ha-not-so-much-dot-com!'
jokes.setup: Chandler is leaving for Tulsa still stinging about Jeffrey; he takes one last shot
jokes.punchline: The invented email address 'www.ha-ha-not-so-much.com' — a 2003-era internet joke about dismissing rival humor
jokes.explanation: A period-specific internet joke that works in context — Chandler's mock website is a decent exit gag. Slightly dated now but functional for its era. The character integration is good: Chandler going out with a dismissive quip rather than confronting his feelings is very him.

jokes.text: Monica finally admits Jeffrey 'still kills me' and 'a little pee came out'
jokes.setup: Monica told Chandler that Jeffrey told a sexist joke and wasn't funny anymore
jokes.punchline: The moment Chandler leaves, Monica admits to Rachel that Jeffrey still kills her and she almost lost control of her bladder laughing
jokes.explanation: Good reversal — Monica lied to Chandler about Jeffrey to spare his feelings, then immediately reveals the truth. The specific 'a little pee came out' is both funny in its specificity and a great measure of extreme laughter. Structural payoff to the Jeffrey subplot.

jokes.text: Rachel watches from the door as Ross goes to fire Sandy: 'I can't watch. It's like firing Elmo.'
jokes.setup: Ross is approaching Sandy to fire him
jokes.punchline: 'It's like firing Elmo' — Rachel uses the most sympathetic Muppet character as a comparison for Sandy
jokes.explanation: Good pop-culture simile. Elmo is specifically the right choice — not just any Muppet but the most innocent, lovable, big-eyed one. It captures Sandy's gentle quality perfectly.

jokes.text: Sandy says he picked Ross and Rachel because he 'liked them best' out of many offers — 'Oh, damn you, Geller!'
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to feel okay about firing Sandy; Sandy reveals he chose them specifically because he liked them
jokes.punchline: Ross's involuntary 'Oh, damn you, Geller!' — a self-directed curse at his own guilt
jokes.explanation: Ross cursing himself in third person is a great comedic choice — 'damn you, Geller!' captures his trapped guilt perfectly. The third-person self-address is both funny and character-specific.

jokes.text: 'And my father walks in and says, What are you doing with those things? What's wrong with you? Why aren't you outside playing like a real boy?'
jokes.setup: Ross is tearfully recounting his childhood under Sandy's therapy-style questioning
jokes.punchline: The dinosaur toys in his apartment suddenly mean much more — this is why they're Ross's, not Emma's
jokes.explanation: Callback to the dinosaur toys pays off beautifully here — now they have an emotional backstory. The joke is both funny and oddly poignant: Ross's attachment to dinosaurs is lifelong resistance to his father's criticism. This rewatch bonus is real — the toys scene hits differently on second viewing.

jokes.text: 'But you are a real boy.' / 'I know I am! And when it's summer and it's hot, why can't you wear a tank top?!'
jokes.setup: Sandy sympathetically affirms Ross's worth after his father's criticism
jokes.punchline: Ross's raw emotional outburst escalates from dinosaurs to tank tops — a surprisingly mundane grievance delivered with maximum intensity
jokes.explanation: The escalation from emotionally resonant (dinosaurs/father's approval) to trivially petty (tank tops) is a classic comedic gear shift. 'Why can't you wear a tank top?!' hitting with the same emotional force as serious childhood trauma is the joke. The bathetic drop is perfectly calibrated.

jokes.text: 'It's all right. Crying is good. It lets the boo-hoos out.'
jokes.setup: Ross is now fully crying in front of the nanny he was about to fire
jokes.punchline: Sandy comforts Ross with 'it lets the boo-hoos out' — condescending baby-talk delivered to a grown man
jokes.explanation: 'Boo-hoos' is a nanny phrase applied to an adult in crisis — the register mismatch is perfect. Sandy treating Ross exactly like Emma is the joke, and it's well-earned by this point.

jokes.text: 'Here comes some more!'
jokes.setup: Sandy has just said crying is good; Ross appears to be stabilizing
jokes.punchline: Sandy sees another wave coming and announces it cheerfully
jokes.explanation: Good button — Sandy's cheerful professionalism about incoming emotional waves is both funny and consistent with his character. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: 'Emma, one day you're gonna grow up and be a big girl, just like your daddy.'
jokes.setup: Sandy is soothing Emma while Ross cries
jokes.punchline: Sandy inadvertently (or deliberately?) says Emma will grow up to be a big girl 'just like her daddy' — referencing Ross's current emotional state
jokes.explanation: The phrasing is deliciously ambiguous — is Sandy commenting on Ross crying, or just confused about gender? Either way, it lands. Good economy.

jokes.text: Sandy tells Emma about friendship: 'What's the one kind of boat that can never ever sink? A friend ship!'
jokes.setup: Sandy is calmly teaching Emma about friendship after Ross's crying session
jokes.punchline: 'A friend ship' — a genuinely corny pun delivered with Sandy's earnest warmth
jokes.explanation: An intentionally corny, preschool-level pun — the joke is that Sandy is saying this to a 2-month-old who cannot understand it. The humor is in the earnestness, not the pun itself. Weak as a joke but functions as character illustration.

jokes.text: 'Wow! You blow my mind!'
jokes.setup: Sandy has just told Emma the 'friend ship' pun
jokes.punchline: Ross's deadpan 'Wow! You blow my mind!' — sarcastic awe at the corniness
jokes.explanation: Ross's mock-amazement is a decent reaction beat. The sarcasm is clear but not especially inventive.

jokes.text: 'How much do I owe you?' / 'Twenty bucks.' / 'It's like the cheapest college ever!'
jokes.setup: Sandy is packing up to leave; Ross asks what he owes
jokes.punchline: Ross — just having had an emotional breakdown and breakthrough — describes the session as 'the cheapest college ever'
jokes.explanation: Smart exit line — Ross reframes his unexpected therapy session as an educational investment. 'Cheapest college ever' captures his academic framing and his emotional journey in one tidy, funny phrase.

jokes.text: 'Okay, bye-bye, Skadandy.' — Joey to Sandy
jokes.setup: Sandy is leaving
jokes.punchline: Joey calls Sandy 'Skadandy' — the same name the child Daniel used for Sandy, which Sandy shared as a touching story
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode-closing callback. Joey using 'Skadandy' — which Sandy shared as an emotional memory — with cheerful casualness is both funny and heartwarming. It lands as an affectionate gesture from Joey that also circles back to the episode's emotional core. Well-earned.

jokes.text: Sandy: 'Okay, bye-bye, Skadandy.' [leaving — using the nickname the previous child gave him, which made him cry in the interview]
jokes.setup: Sandy's farewell to Ross and the apartment
jokes.punchline: He uses the nickname 'Skadandy' — the same word that made him cry in the interview (joke #25) — but now on himself as a self-aware farewell
jokes.explanation: A satisfying full-circle callback. Sandy using 'Skadandy' as his own farewell recontextualizes the name from tragic to endearing. It also implies he's begun a similar bond with this household despite being fired. Good structural awareness by the writers.

tmdb_overview: Ross and Rachel hire a nanny for Emma named Sandy and things seem to be going great. However, Ross is uncomfortable having a male nanny. Meanwhile, Chandler becomes upset when Monica says that somebody from her new job is the funniest guy she's ever met. Also, after Phoebe and Mike  decide to take their relationship to a new level and exchange apartment keys, Phoebe gets a surprise visit from her ex-boyfriend David.
insight: Male nanny premise sustains 65 jokes at 2.5 per minute, anchoring Season 9's character-driven phase.
